cards.text: Micah, a prophet, has just looked around and found no one upright left. But as for him, he says he will wait for the God of his salvation. Now he turns and speaks to his enemy: "Do not gloat over me, my enemy!"

cards.question: True or false: Micah tells his enemy that now that he's fallen, he's staying down.
Micah sits in darkness, but he says the LORD will be his ___.

cards.text: Then Micah owns it: he has sinned against the LORD, so he must endure the LORD's rage. No excuses. No "traffic was CRAZY."

cards.question: Micah says he must endure the LORD's rage. Until when?

answers.text: Until the LORD argues his case
Until he pays back every debt

cards.text: Now back to that enemy. She's the one who taunted Micah, "Where is the LORD your God?"

cards.question: When the enemy who taunted Micah sees what the LORD does for him, what covers her?

cards.text: Micah says that at that time she'll be trampled like mud in the streets. Lesson learned, friend: don't trash-talk somebody right before their God shows up.

cards.question: Then the message turns to "you": the day will come for ___ your walls and extending your boundary.

cards.text: On that day they come from Assyria, a powerful empire, and from the cities of Egypt, from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. That's not a guest list, friend. That's the WHOLE MAP.

cards.question: Then Micah says the earth will become desolate. Why?

answers.text: Because of what its people did
Because its walls were never built

cards.text: Then comes a prayer to the LORD: shepherd Your people with Your staff, the flock of Your inheritance. Let them graze in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old.

cards.question: Then God speaks. He'll show His wonders, just like in the days when His people came out of ___.

cards.text: The nations see it and are ashamed, stripped of all their might. Hands over their mouths, ears gone deaf. That's me, mustache over my mouth, every time I hit "reply all" by accident.

cards.question: The nations lick the dust like a snake. True or false: then they come trembling out of their strongholds in fear of the LORD.

cards.text: Then Micah asks the big one: "Who is a God like You," who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance? Go ahead, look around, friend. Nobody's raising their hand.

cards.question: Micah says God does not hold on to His anger forever. Why not?

answers.text: His people finally earned it back
He forgets what His people did

cards.text: Micah says God will again have compassion on us, vanquish our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. Notice that "us," friend: Micah's not up front pointing fingers, he's standing in line WITH everybody.

cards.question: Micah pictures God casting all our sins into the depths of the sea. What is that picture saying?

answers.text: Those sins are gone for good
Those sins will wash back up
Those sins are saved for later

cards.question: Micah ends with God showing faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, Jacob's grandfather (Genesis 21:3; 25:26). True or false: Micah says God does this just as He swore to their fathers from the days of old.

findings.problem: This story card only paraphrases Micah 7:14 and has nothing of Papa Dorin's voice. No reaction, comparison, storyteller line or humor, so it reads as stripped down.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "He forgets what His people did" is arguably right. Micah 7:18 says God "passes over the transgression," and 7:19 pictures sins cast into the depths of the sea. Card 19 then treats "those sins are gone for good" as correct. A baker could argue that forgetting is why God does not keep His anger forever.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Jacob appears for the first time in this walkthrough and isn't introduced. Abraham is introduced only through Jacob ("Jacob's grandfather"), and Jacob himself is never identified.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The walkthrough names the "I" of Micah 7:8-10 and the "us" of 7:19 as Micah himself (cards 1, 2, 4, 6, 18). The text doesn't name the speaker. The enemy is "she," and 7:11 addresses a "you" whose walls will be rebuilt. Many readers take 7:8-10 as Zion or Israel speaking, not Micah personally. Card 18's line "Micah's not up front pointing fingers, he's standing in line WITH everybody" depends on reading the speaker as Micah. The "Who's speaking" rule requires naming the speaker. "Leave open what the text leaves open" covers who is being spoken to, but it doesn't say what to do when the speaker of a prophetic passage is unnamed.
findings.question: When the speaker of a prophetic passage isn't named and could be the prophet or the personified people or city, should Papa Dorin name the prophet as the speaker, or use something neutral like "the speaker" or "God's people," and drop lines like card 18's that rely on the speaker being Micah?
